KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and seasonable through mid-week. Some 
patchy frost possible tonight.

High pressure over the Gulf Coast states will build east through
the middle of the week before moving offshore on Wednesday.
Tranquil conditions expected during this period.

The pressure gradient tightens once again today, and west to
northwest winds will increase to around 15 mph with gusts to
around 20 mph this afternoon. Winds diminish tonight. Highs
today will be a bit warmer than they were on Monday, topping off
in the low to mid 60s. 

Under clear skies and with light to nearly calm winds, lows 
tonight will drop into the 30s to low 40s. Suppose some patchy 
frost is possible where the growing season remains active across
portions of southern NJ and into the Delmarva. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strengthening storm system will impact the 
region Thursday through Friday night.

A vigorous upper-level trough continues to be forecast to 
evolve across the eastern U.S. later this week and into the 
weekend. This supports a surface low that strengthens as it 
tracks across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic region. The main 
low main tracks into the Ohio Valley while a secondary low 
develops in the vicinity of the northern Mid-Atlantic. The model
guidance, including ensemble data, continues to be in good 
agreement that a deep upper-level trough evolves in the East 
later this week. There are however some differences remaining 
with the handling of the embedded shortwaves and thus the 
details of the surface low. This will determine whether the 
strengthening storm tracks over our region or slides just south 
and then east/offshore. Despite the continued uncertainty on the
finer details, our region will still be impacted by a storm.

The strength of the parent upper-level trough results in a 
colder air mass moving in with time, however the initial air 
mass is not all that cold (the lack of a cold antecedent air 
mass). The air mass may become sufficiently cold enough on the 
west to northwestern edge of the precipitation shield for a 
rain/snow mix or even some snow across the higher elevations of 
our far western to northwest zones, confined particularly to the
southern Poconos. Otherwise, a rain event is forecast. The 
amount of precipitation (rain and/or snow) will depend on the 
ultimate development and track of the main surface low. The GEFS
and ECMWF members suggest a spread still with the 
placement/track of the surface low, however overall this looks 
to be mostly a rain event for the majority of our region. The 
coastal impacts, including the potential for stronger winds and 
also tidal flooding, are less certain because if the surface low
tracks right over our area that would lessen the residence time
of the (stronger) onshore flow. If an inland track to the 
surface low occurs, then portions of our area could get briefly 
into some milder air and therefore some thunder would be 
possible. The strongest winds with this may end up occurring as 
the storm exits and the cold air advection then increases from 
the northwest. The main uncertainty is on how much precipitation
occurs with this event and the extent of any higher elevation 
snowfall (southern Poconos). 


KEY MESSAGE 3...A stretch of below normal temperatures begins 
on Friday, continuing through the weekend as a much colder 
airmass moves overhead. 

In the wake of the storm, as it deepens and tracks toward the 
Canadian Maritimes over the weekend, a colder air mass will be 
in place across our area. In addition, a tightened pressure 
gradient coupled with deeper mixing should result in a period of
breezy to windy conditions over the weekend. Daytime 
temperatures on Friday and Saturday should not get out of the 
40s for many areas, with temperatures at night dropping into the
20s to low 30s. Some areas likely will see their first freeze 
of the season as the growing season is still active across 
Delmarva, parts of South Jersey, and far southeastern 
Pennsylvania. There could even be some lake effect snow and/or 
rain showers into the southern Poconos on Saturday but things 
like dry for the most part elsewhere. 

Temperatures should moderate some on Sunday and Monday, but the
current forecast still has temperatures in the upper 40s/low 
50s each day, which would still be below normal for mid-
November.
